claim: C-mannosylation takes place in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), presumably co-translationally.
source: It takes place in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), presumably co-translationally (Doucey et al., 1998; Krieg et al., 1998), and is performed by C-mannosyltransferase enzymes of the DPY(dumpy)-19 family (Buettner et al., 2013; Niwa et al., 2016; Shcherbakova et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Doucey et al., 1998; Krieg et al., 1998)

claim: C-mannosylation is performed by C-mannosyltransferase enzymes of the DPY(dumpy)-19 family.
source: It takes place in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), presumably co-translationally (Doucey et al., 1998; Krieg et al., 1998), and is performed by C-mannosyltransferase enzymes of the DPY(dumpy)-19 family (Buettner et al., 2013; Niwa et al., 2016; Shcherbakova et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Buettner et al., 2013; Niwa et al., 2016; Shcherbakova et al., 2017)

claim: C-mannosylation has been found on tryptophans of WXXW/C motifs.
source: C-mannosylation has been found on tryptophans of WXXW/C motifs and involves a carbon-carbon linkage between the sugar and the protein: the C1 atom of the α-mannose is thereby attached to the indole C2 atom of the tryptophan (Figure 1A) (de Beer et al., 1995; Hofsteenge et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (de Beer et al., 1995; Hofsteenge et al., 1994)

claim: C-mannosylation involves a carbon-carbon linkage between the C1 atom of the α-mannose and the indole C2 atom of the tryptophan.
source: C-mannosylation has been found on tryptophans of WXXW/C motifs and involves a carbon-carbon linkage between the sugar and the protein: the C1 atom of the α-mannose is thereby attached to the indole C2 atom of the tryptophan (Figure 1A) (de Beer et al., 1995; Hofsteenge et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations and Figure 1A showing the C-C bond structure

claim: C-mannosylation has been predicted on 18% of human secreted and transmembrane proteins.
source: C-mannosylation has been predicted on 18% of human secreted and transmembrane proteins (Julenius, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Julenius, 2007

claim: TSRs are small protein domains consisting of around 60 amino acids.
source: TSRs are small protein domains consisting of around 60 amino acids.
evidence: Supported by citation to Tan et al., 2002

claim: TSRs possess a conserved structure of three antiparallel strands typically linked by three disulfide bridges.
source: They possess a conserved structure of three antiparallel strands typically linked by three disulfide bridges (Figure 1B) (Tan et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tan et al., 2002 and Figure 1B showing the structure

claim: The first strand of TSRs contains the C-mannosylation motif with up to three tryptophan residues (WXXWXXWXXC), which all can be C-mannosylated.
source: The first strand contains the C-mannosylation motif with up to three tryptophan residues (WXXWXXWXXC), which all can be C-mannosylated (Hofsteenge et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hofsteenge et al., 1999

claim: The tryptophans in TSRs intercalate with conserved arginine residues from the second strand building a tryptophan-arginine (Trp-Arg) ladder that forms the core of the TSR fold.
source: The tryptophans intercalate with conserved arginine residues from the second strand building a so-called tryptophan-arginine (Trp-Arg) ladder that forms the core of the TSR fold (Figure 1B) (Tan et al., 2002; Tossavainen et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tan et al., 2002; Tossavainen et al., 2006 and Figure 1B

claim: The Trp-Arg ladder is deduced to have an important structural function in the TSRs due to stabilizing cation-π interactions between the arginine and tryptophan side chains.
source: Due to stabilizing cation-π interactions between the arginine and tryptophan side chains (Gallivan and Dougherty, 1999), the Trp-Arg ladder is deduced to have an important structural function in the TSRs.
evidence: Supported by citation to Gallivan and Dougherty, 1999 and inference about structural function

claim: Mutagenesis of the C-mannosylation sites usually resulted in reduced secretion or cell-surface expression of the proteins and their retention in the ER.
source: Mutagenesis of the C-mannosylation sites usually resulted in reduced secretion or cell-surface expression of the proteins and their retention in the ER (Fujiwara et al., 2016; Gouyer et al., 2018; Hilton et al., 1996; Niwa et al., 2016; Okamoto et al., 2017; Sasazawa et al., 2015; Taylor et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: Lack of C-mannosylation alone was responsible for reduced secretion of TSR-containing proteins.
source: This indeed allowed to demonstrate that lack of C-mannosylation alone was responsible for reduced secretion of TSR-containing proteins (Buettner et al., 2013; Niwa et al., 2016; Shcherbakova et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Buettner et al., 2013; Niwa et al., 2016; Shcherbakova et al., 2017

claim: At 20°C, secretion of UNC-5 TSRs was higher from cells co-expressing DPY-19 than from C-mannosylation-negative cells.
source: At 20°C, secretion of UNC-5 TSRs was higher from cells co-expressing DPY-19 than from C-mannosylation-negative cells (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: At increasing temperatures, secretion of C-mannosylated TSRs was not affected, whereas secretion of non-mannosylated TSRs further declined gradually.
source: At increasing temperatures, secretion of C-mannosylated TSRs was not affected, whereas secretion of non-mannosylated TSRs further declined gradually.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: Intracellular UNC-5 TSR levels were comparable at all conditions confirming that the cells were able to produce C- and non-mannosylated TSRs per se.
source: Intracellular UNC-5 TSR levels were comparable at all conditions confirming that the cells were able to produce C- and non-mannosylated TSRs per se (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: Impaired temperature-dependent secretion of non-mannosylated TSRs implied a role of C-mannoses in protein stability and/or protein folding.
source: Thus, impaired temperature-dependent secretion of non-mannosylated TSRs implied a role of C-mannoses in protein stability and/or protein folding.
evidence: Inference based on experimental observations of temperature-dependent secretion

claim: The major fraction of UNC-5 TSR2 was modified on the first two tryptophans of the WXXWXXW motif.
source: Presence of C-mannoses was verified by mass spectrometry, showing that the major fraction of the protein was modified on the first two tryptophans of the WXXWXXW motif (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Both C-mannosylated and non-mannosylated UNC-5 TSR2 display TSR-typical CD spectra with characteristic maxima near 230 and 212 nm and a minimum in the 195–200 nm region.
source: The correct folding of both TSR forms was confirmed by circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy showing TSR-typical spectra with characteristic maxima near 230 and 212 nm and a minimum in the 195–200 nm region (Figure 3A) (Huwiler et al., 2002; Roszmusz et al., 2002; Smith et al., 1984).
evidence: Supported by CD spectroscopy data in Figure 3A and citations to previous studies

claim: The C-mannosylated TSR revealed a significantly higher melting temperature (Tm = 59.5°C) compared to the non-mannosylated form (Tm = 50.4°C).
source: The C-mannosylated TSR revealed a significantly higher melting temperature (Tm = 59.5°C) compared to the non-mannosylated form (Tm = 50.4°C) showing that C-mannosylation on W1 and W2 of the WXXWXXW motif strongly increases the resistance of the TSR to thermal denaturation.
evidence: Supported by thermal denaturation data shown in Figure 3B

claim: C-mannosylation on W1 and W2 of the WXXWXXW motif strongly increases the resistance of the TSR to thermal denaturation.
source: The C-mannosylated TSR revealed a significantly higher melting temperature (Tm = 59.5°C) compared to the non-mannosylated form (Tm = 50.4°C) showing that C-mannosylation on W1 and W2 of the WXXWXXW motif strongly increases the resistance of the TSR to thermal denaturation.
evidence: Inference based on melting temperature data

claim: Positions of arginines and tryptophans in the C-mannosylated TSR remained more constrained in all three simulation replicates.
source: However, positions of arginines and tryptophans in the C-mannosylated TSR remained more constrained in all three simulation replicates (Figure 4A) indicating that the Trp-Arg ladder structure in the C-mannosylated TSR is more rigid compared to the non-modified TSR.
evidence: Supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 4A

claim: The Trp-Arg ladder structure in the C-mannosylated TSR is more rigid compared to the non-modified TSR.
source: However, positions of arginines and tryptophans in the C-mannosylated TSR remained more constrained in all three simulation replicates (Figure 4A) indicating that the Trp-Arg ladder structure in the C-mannosylated TSR is more rigid compared to the non-modified TSR.
evidence: Inference based on molecular dynamics simulation data

claim: Trp5 appeared highly flexible and diverged from the residual Trp-Arg ladder organization in the non-mannosylated form.
source: Particularly Trp5 – the first tryptophan of the WXXWXXW motif – appeared highly flexible and diverged from the residual Trp-Arg ladder organization in the non-mannosylated form (Figure 4—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 4 and videos

claim: Calculated cation-π interactions between Trp5 and Arg24 were found to be maintained in the C-mannosylated TSR but not in the non-modified TSR.
source: Correspondingly, calculated cation-π interactions between Trp5 and Arg24 were found to be maintained in the C-mannosylated TSR but not in the non-modified TSR (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: Hydrogen bond interactions between C-mannoses and the neighboring side chains as well as the backbone of the corresponding tryptophan residues were found throughout the simulations.
source: Furthermore, we found hydrogen bond interactions between C-mannoses and the neighboring side chains as well as the backbone of the corresponding tryptophan residues throughout the simulations (Figure 4C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 4C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 4

claim: C-mannoses appeared to keep the tryptophans in specific orientations not only by affecting their conformational space but also by forming polar interactions with surrounding residues.
source: Thus, C-mannoses appeared to keep the tryptophans in specific orientations not only by affecting their conformational space but also by forming polar interactions with surrounding residues.
evidence: Inference based on hydrogen bond analysis from simulations

claim: Denaturation of the C-mannosylated TSR occurred approximately 1.8 times slower than that of the non-mannosylated repeat under reducing conditions.
source: Denaturation of the C-mannosylated TSR, however, occurred approximately 1.8 times slower than that of the non-mannosylated repeat (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by reductive denaturation data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Non-mannosylated TSR revealed an increased flexibility of Trp5 in the Trp-Arg ladder organization in comparison to the C-mannosylated TSR in simulations lacking disulfide bonds.
source: As in the thermal denaturation simulation, non-mannosylated TSR revealed an increased flexibility of Trp5 in the Trp-Arg ladder organization in comparison to the C-mannosylated TSR (Figure 5B,C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 5B,C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Cys26 involved in the upper disulfide bridge showed lower fluctuation values and thus decreased flexibility in the C-mannosylated TSR.
source: Additionally, Cys26 (marked by *) involved in the upper disulfide bridge showed lower fluctuation values and thus decreased flexibility in the C-mannosylated TSR (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) which might be relevant for the disulfide bond formation during protein folding.
evidence: Supported by RMSF data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Both C-mannosylated and non-mannosylated TSRs were able to form native-like conformations during oxidative folding.
source: Both TSRs were able to form native-like conformations as demonstrated by the appearance of the characteristic TSR peak in CD spectra (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Folding initiation of the C-mannosylated TSR occurred significantly faster compared to the non-modified protein.
source: Still, folding initiation of the C-mannosylated TSR occured significantly faster compared to the non-modified protein (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), confirming that C-mannosylation plays a role in the folding of UNC-5 TSR2.
evidence: Supported by oxidative folding data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: C-mannosylation plays a role in the folding of UNC-5 TSR2.
source: Still, folding initiation of the C-mannosylated TSR occured significantly faster compared to the non-modified protein (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), confirming that C-mannosylation plays a role in the folding of UNC-5 TSR2.
evidence: Inference based on oxidative folding data

claim: Non-mannosylated TSR revealed a high amount of dimeric structures connected by aberrant disulfides.
source: Whereas C-mannosylated TSR2 appeared primary as monomer (a), non-mannosylated TSR revealed a high amount of dimeric structures (b), which bound stronger to the nickel affinity column and were confirmed by gel filtration chromatography and non-reducing SDS-PAGE.
evidence: Supported by purification data shown in Figure 6B

claim: In cells co-expressing DPY-19 C-mannosyltransferase, dimeric TSR formation was significantly reduced.
source: In cells co-expressing DPY-19 C-mannosyltransferase, dimeric TSR formation was significantly reduced.
evidence: Supported by purification data shown in Figure 6B

claim: C-mannoses added on the first two tryptophans of the WXXWXXW motif affect the dynamics of a TSR and play an important role in its folding, stability and secretion.
source: In the present study, we compared non- and C-mannosylated UNC-5 TSRs and were able to show that C-mannoses added on the first two tryptophans of the WXXWXXW motif affect the dynamics of a TSR and play an important role in its folding, stability and secretion.
evidence: Conclusion based on multiple experimental results presented in the study

claim: C-mannosylation is co-translational.
source: Assuming that C-mannosylation is co-translational (Krieg et al., 1998) implies that it precedes and thereby assists correct Cys pairing to form the native disulfide bridges.
evidence: Supported by citation to Krieg et al., 1998

claim: C-mannosylation precedes and thereby assists correct Cys pairing to form the native disulfide bridges.
source: Assuming that C-mannosylation is co-translational (Krieg et al., 1998) implies that it precedes and thereby assists correct Cys pairing to form the native disulfide bridges.
evidence: Inference based on co-translational nature of C-mannosylation and experimental observations

claim: Increased formation of covalent dimers was observed for TSR2 of C. elegans UNC-5 in the absence of C-mannosylation, which were caused by incorrect disulfide bond connections.
source: Indeed, we observed increased formation of covalent dimers (Figure 6B) for TSR2 of C. elegans UNC-5 in the absence of C-mannosylation, which were caused by incorrect disulfide bond connections.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The Trp-Arg ladder most likely plays an essential role in the correct positioning of cysteines.
source: The Trp-Arg ladder most likely plays an essential role in the correct positioning of cysteines.
evidence: Inference based on simulation and experimental data

claim: The mannoses assist in the formation of the ladder and stabilize it before disulfide bridges are made.
source: It is conceivable that the mannoses assist in the formation of the ladder and stabilize it before disulfide bridges are made.
evidence: Inference based on simulation and experimental data

claim: Oxidative folding experiments showed that the refolding initiation (appearance of the Trp-Arg ladder) was accelerated by the presence of C-mannoses.
source: Our oxidative folding experiments indeed showed that the refolding initiation (appearance of the Trp-Arg ladder) was accelerated by the presence of C-mannoses (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by oxidative folding data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Protein domain folding precedes disulfide bridge formation.
source: This is also consistent with the view that protein domain folding precedes disulfide bridge formation (Robinson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Robinson et al., 2017

claim: C-mannosylated TSR was more resistant to thermal denaturation than non-mannosylated TSR.
source: Nevertheless, C-mannosylated TSR was more resistant to thermal denaturation than non-mannosylated TSR (Figure 3B) revealing the importance of C-mannosylation also after folding of the TSR.
evidence: Supported by thermal denaturation data shown in Figure 3B

claim: C-mannoses were able to build hydrogen bonds to the surrounding residues and kept especially the tryptophan closest to the N-terminus in place.
source: Molecular dynamics simulations at elevated temperature showed that C-mannoses were able to built hydrogen bonds to the surrounding residues (Figure 4C,D) and kept especially the tryptophan closest to the N-terminus in place.
evidence: Supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 4C,D

claim: Without C-mannose, the first tryptophan was consistently losing its proper orientation in the ladder in repeated simulations, resulting in higher flexibility of the upper TSR region.
source: Without C-mannose, this tryptophan was consistently losing its proper orientation in the ladder in repeated simulations, resulting in higher flexibility of the upper TSR region (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 4A,B

claim: Existence of hydrogen bonds between C-mannoses and surrounding amino acids was suggested in recent structural studies on properdin.
source: Existence of hydrogen bonds between C-mannoses and surrounding amino acids was also suggested in recent structural studies on properdin (Pedersen et al., 2019; Pronker et al., 2016; van den Bos et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent structural studies

claim: The C. elegans C-mannosyltransferase DPY-19 is not targeting the third tryptophan in UNC-5.
source: Since the C. elegans C-mannosyltransferase DPY-19 is not targeting this tryptophan, it remains unmodified in C. elegans UNC-5.
evidence: Inference based on experimental observations

claim: In mammals, the third tryptophan of the WXXWXXWXXC sequence can be mannosylated by the DPY19L3 homolog.
source: In mammals, the third tryptophan of the WXXWXXWXXC sequence can be mannosylated by the DPY19L3 homolog (Hofsteenge et al., 1999; Shcherbakova et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hofsteenge et al., 1999; Shcherbakova et al., 2017

claim: Secretion of human R-spondin1 was highly reduced in DPY19L3-restricted cells.
source: Secretion of human R-spondin1 was highly reduced in DPY19L3-restricted cells (Niwa et al., 2016), whereas mouse UNC5A was not affected (Shcherbakova et al., 2017).

claim: Mouse UNC5A was not affected by DPY19L3 restriction.
source: Secretion of human R-spondin1 was highly reduced in DPY19L3-restricted cells (Niwa et al., 2016), whereas mouse UNC5A was not affected (Shcherbakova et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shcherbakova et al., 2017

claim: Multiple TSRs have been produced in native conformations in bacteria or insect cells without glycosylation.
source: On the other hand, multiple TSRs have been produced in native conformations in bacteria or insect cells without glycosylation (Klenotic et al., 2011; Tan et al., 2002; Tossavainen et al., 2006), showing that C-mannosylation is probably not an absolute requirement for some TSRs, but a critical factor for others.
evidence: Supported by citations to Klenotic et al., 2011; Tan et al., 2002; Tossavainen et al., 2006

claim: C-mannosylation is probably not an absolute requirement for some TSRs, but a critical factor for others.
source: On the other hand, multiple TSRs have been produced in native conformations in bacteria or insect cells without glycosylation (Klenotic et al., 2011; Tan et al., 2002; Tossavainen et al., 2006), showing that C-mannosylation is probably not an absolute requirement for some TSRs, but a critical factor for others.

claim: C. elegans dpy-19 mutants deficient in C-mannosylation develop a temperature-sensitive dumpy phenotype.
source: C. elegans dpy-19 mutants deficient in C-mannosylation develop a temperature-sensitive dumpy phenotype (Honigberg and Kenyon, 2000) that we could reproduce (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: In C. elegans dpy-19 mutants, secretion and stability of various TSR-containing and possibly other proteins are affected.
source: We assume that in these mutants, secretion and stability of various TSR-containing and possibly other proteins are affected.

claim: Impairment of UNC-5 alone is not sufficient for the development of the dumpy phenotype.
source: Since impairment of UNC-5 alone is not sufficient for the development of the dumpy phenotype (Hedgecock et al., 1990), further C-mannosylation-dependent proteins must be involved.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hedgecock et al., 1990

claim: C-mannosylation of tryptophans in the Trp-Arg ladder of TSRs can provide assistance in the folding process and greatly enhance the stability of the folded protein.
source: In conclusion, our experiments support a model in which C-mannosylation of tryptophans in the Trp-Arg ladder of TSRs can provide assistance in the folding process, but also greatly enhance the stability of the folded protein.

claim: Drosophila S2 cells are naturally C-mannose-negative.

claim: C-mannosylation of the TSRs was obtained by co-expression of the C. elegans DPY-19 C-mannosyltransferase.
source: C-mannosylation of the TSRs was obtained by co-expression of the C. elegans DPY-19 C-mannosyltransferase.

claim: Thermal denaturation of both non- and C-mannosylated TSRs was reversible to a high extent.
source: Thermal denaturation of both, non- and C-mannosylated TSRs, was reversible to a high extent (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: C-mannoses can occur in 4C1 and 1C4 forms.
source: However, because NMR studies (de Beer et al., 1995; Nishikawa et al., 2005) and recently resolved TSR crystal structures (Pedersen et al., 2019; Pronker et al., 2016; van den Bos et al., 2019) suggest that C-mannoses can occur in 4C1 and 1C4 forms, we also performed a simulation with C-mannoses in 1C4-chair arrangement (Figure 4—video 3).

claim: For both 4C1 and 1C4 conformations, similar maintenance of the Trp-Arg ladder and ability to form hydrogen bonds was observed.
source: For both conformations, we observed similar maintenance of the Trp-Arg ladder and ability to form hydrogen bonds (Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4).

claim: Upon addition of 2 mM DTT, both C-mannosylated and non-mannosylated proteins started to unfold immediately, showing that the disulfides are essential for the TSR structure.
source: Upon addition of 2 mM DTT, both proteins started to unfold immediately, showing that the disulfides are essential for the TSR structure.

claim: C-mannosylation might decrease the accessibility of the disulfide bridges by DTT, but could also protect the Trp-Arg ladder organization of the TSR.
source: C-mannosylation might decrease the accessibility of the disulfide bridges by DTT, but could also protect the Trp-Arg ladder organization of the TSR.

claim: The disulfide bridges are essential for the TSR structure.
source: Upon addition of 2 mM DTT, both proteins started to unfold immediately, showing that the disulfides are essential for the TSR structure.

claim: Highly increased formation of dimers was consistently observed in over ten independent purifications of non-mannosylated TSR2.
source: Highly increased formation of dimers was consistently observed in over ten independent purifications.

claim: The first TSR of C. elegans MIG-21 lacks two of the six cysteines and might require C-mannosylation since it cannot be secreted without C-mannoses even at low temperatures.
source: In C. elegans MIG-21, the first TSR lacks two of the six cysteines and might, therefore, require C-mannosylation since it cannot be secreted without C-mannoses even at low temperatures (Buettner et al., 2013).

claim: The requirement for C-mannosylation at the third tryptophan position, as well as on the first two tryptophans, might vary in different organisms and different proteins.
source: The requirement for C-mannosylation at this position, as well as on the first two tryptophans, might thus vary in different organisms and different proteins.

claim: C-mannoses orient the underlying tryptophan residues and facilitate the formation of the tryptophan-arginine ladder in the endoplasmic reticulum folding process.
source: We propose that in the endoplasmic reticulum folding process, C-mannoses orient the underlying tryptophan residues and facilitate the formation of the tryptophan-arginine ladder, thereby influencing the positioning of cysteines and disulfide bridging.

claim: C-mannoses influence the positioning of cysteines and disulfide bridging.
source: We propose that in the endoplasmic reticulum folding process, C-mannoses orient the underlying tryptophan residues and facilitate the formation of the tryptophan-arginine ladder, thereby influencing the positioning of cysteines and disulfide bridging.
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental and simulation data

claim: C-mannoses can be involved in intramolecular hydrogen bonding and limit the flexibility of the TSR tryptophan-arginine ladder.
source: Molecular dynamics simulations supported the experimental studies and showed that C-mannoses can be involved in intramolecular hydrogen bonding and limit the flexibility of the TSR tryptophan-arginine ladder.

claim: In absence of C-mannosylation, UNC-5 TSRs could only be obtained at low temperature.
source: In absence of C-mannosylation, UNC-5 TSRs could only be obtained at low temperature and a significant proportion displayed incorrect intermolecular disulfide bridging, which was hardly observed when C-mannosylated.

claim: A significant proportion of non-C-mannosylated UNC-5 TSRs displayed incorrect intermolecular disulfide bridging, which was hardly observed when C-mannosylated.
source: In absence of C-mannosylation, UNC-5 TSRs could only be obtained at low temperature and a significant proportion displayed incorrect intermolecular disulfide bridging, which was hardly observed when C-mannosylated.
evidence: Experimental observation from the study

claim: Glycosylated TSRs exhibited higher resistance to thermal and reductive denaturation processes.
source: Glycosylated TSRs exhibited higher resistance to thermal and reductive denaturation processes, and the presence of C-mannoses promoted the oxidative folding of a reduced and denatured TSR in vitro.

claim: The presence of C-mannoses promoted the oxidative folding of a reduced and denatured TSR in vitro.
source: Glycosylated TSRs exhibited higher resistance to thermal and reductive denaturation processes, and the presence of C-mannoses promoted the oxidative folding of a reduced and denatured TSR in vitro.

claim: Protein glycosylation affects the majority of secreted and cell-surface proteins.
source: Protein glycosylation is a major form of co- and post-translational modification, affecting the majority of secreted and cell-surface proteins.

claim: Protein glycosylation can influence the folding of a protein as well as its physical properties, activity and ability to interact with other macromolecules.
source: It can influence the folding of a protein as well as its physical properties, activity and ability to interact with other macromolecules, thus playing an important role in a great variety of cellular processes (Varki, 2017).

claim: C-mannosylation is presently one of the less well characterized glycosylation types.
source: C-mannosylation is presently one of the less well characterized glycosylation types.

claim: There are two main protein groups bearing conserved C-mannosylation sites – proteins with thrombospondin type 1 repeats (TSRs) and type I cytokine receptors.
source: There are two main protein groups bearing conserved C-mannosylation sites – proteins with thrombospondin type 1 repeats (TSRs) and type I cytokine receptors.
